Sparse Mixtures for Everyone: A Test Paper

Alice Kim, Bob Lee, Carol Park, Dan Choi
Abstract

We propose a sparse mixture of experts model that routes each token to two experts. The model matches a dense baseline while using far fewer FLOPs per token.

Code and checkpoints are released to the community.

1 Introduction

Large language models scale well, but dense computation grows as x2x^{2} for a model of width xx. We propose a sparse mixture of experts model that routes each token to two experts [1, 2]. Knowledge distillation (KD) compresses the router, and the KD loss is cheap.111The router is trained jointly with the experts. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/example/sparse-moe.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a top-two routing rule with a load balancing loss.

  • •

    We show that the model matches a dense baseline on 55 benchmarks while using fewer FLOPs.

Table 1 shows that the sparse model improves accuracy by 2.3 points on MMLU, and Figure 2(a) shows stable training. Routing follows Algorithm 1 and builds on efficient routers [4]. A limitation of our approach is the extra memory required to store all experts (see Appendix A).

2.1 Training objective

We minimize ℒ\mathcal{L} with AdamW and a learning rate of 3×10-43\times 10^{-4}. The balancing coefficient α\alpha is set to 0.01, following prior work [3]. By Theorem 1, uniform routing is optimal.

Theorem 1.

If every expert receives at least one token, the balancing loss is minimized when fi=1/Nf_{i}=1/N.

Proof.

By the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality the sum is minimized at the uniform distribution. ∎
